बरेली में सुबह से तेज धूप, गर्मी और उमस बढ़ी:कल बारिश की संभावना, आज 36 डिग्री तक पहुंच सकता तापमान
- कॉपी लिंक
बरेली में बुधवार सुबह से तेज धूप के चलते गर्मी और उमस बढ़ गई है। आज अधिकतम तापमान 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रह सकता है। सुबह से ही धूप तीखी होने के कारण खुले में लोगों को गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ रहा है।
दोपहर तक तापमान में और बढ़ोतरी होने की संभावना है। गर्मी के साथ हवा में नमी भी लोगों को परेशान कर रही है। IMD के अनुसार, बरेली में आर्द्रता करीब 80 फीसदी दर्ज की गई है। अधिक नमी के कारण पसीना जल्दी नहीं सूख रहा, जिससे 36 डिग्री तापमान भी अधिक गर्म महसूस हो रहा है।
बारिश के बाद बदला मौसम
पिछले दिनों बारिश और बादल रहने से तापमान में कुछ कमी आई थी। अब आसमान साफ होने के साथ धूप तेज हो गई है। बारिश के बाद वातावरण में बनी नमी ने उमस बढ़ा दी है।
IMD के स्थानीय पूर्वानुमान के मुताबिक, 12 अगस्त को आंशिक बादल छाए रह सकते हैं और अधिकतम तापमान करीब 36 डिग्री रह सकता है। 13 अगस्त को तापमान 34 डिग्री तक रहने के साथ गरज-चमक के साथ एक-दो दौर बारिश होने की संभावना है।
धूप में सावधानी जरूरी
तेज धूप के दौरान लंबे समय तक खुले में रहने से बचना बेहतर होगा। जरूरी काम से बाहर निकलते समय सिर ढककर निकलें और पर्याप्त पानी पीते रहें। बच्चों और बुजुर्गों को दोपहर की सीधी धूप से बचाने की जरूरत है।
बुधवार की गर्मी के बाद अगले 24 से 48 घंटे में मौसम में बदलाव के संकेत हैं। 13 अगस्त को बारिश की संभावना के चलते तापमान में कमी आ सकती है। ऐसे में आने वाले दिनों में धूप, बारिश और उमस का दौर बना रहने की उम्मीद है।

कई क्षेत्रों में पानी की कमी तेजी से स्पष्ट होती जा रही है। इटली की पो नदी बेसिन और कई बड़ी झीलों में जलस्तर चिंताजनक रूप से कम हो गया है।
ब्रिटेन में सूखे से 4.5 करोड़ से अधिक लोग प्रभावित हैं, जिनमें से लगभग 27 करोड़ लोग ऐसे क्षेत्रों में रहते हैं जहां पानी पर प्रतिबंध लागू हैं।
इसका प्रभाव केवल आम जनता के जीवन तक ही सीमित नहीं है। सिंचाई के पानी की कमी के कारण कृषि पर दबाव बढ़ रहा है, वहीं राइन और डेन्यूब जैसी प्रमुख नदियों पर परिवहन भी प्रभावित हो रहा है। परमाणु ऊर्जा संयंत्रों सहित कुछ बिजली उत्पादन संयंत्रों को भी जल संसाधनों से संबंधित चुनौतियों का सामना करना पड़ रहा है।
रॉयटर्स ने बताया कि कुछ क्षेत्रों में मक्का और सूरजमुखी जैसी फसलों को नुकसान पहुंचा है। वहीं, यूरोप में जंगल की आग का खतरा ऐतिहासिक रूप से उच्च स्तर पर पहुंच रहा है।
रॉयटर्स द्वारा उद्धृत स्वास्थ्य विशेषज्ञों ने चेतावनी दी है कि अत्यधिक गर्मी को सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य समस्या के रूप में देखा जाना चाहिए। इससे पता चलता है कि जलवायु परिवर्तन का प्रभाव पर्यावरण से कृषि, अर्थव्यवस्था , बुनियादी ढांचे और सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य तक तेजी से फैल रहा है।

हनोई और उत्तरी क्षेत्र में दिन के दौरान भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी, जिसके बाद शाम होते-होते मौसम के मिजाज में बदलाव आएगा।
आज के मौसम पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, हनोई और उत्तरी क्षेत्र में दोपहर और शाम के समय तेज धूप के साथ गर्म मौसम बना रहेगा। दोपहर बाद और शाम को गरज के साथ बारिश होने की संभावना है, जिससे गर्मी से कुछ राहत मिलेगी।
Báo Gia đình và Xã hội•11/08/2026
हनोई और उत्तरी क्षेत्र में गर्म और धूप वाला मौसम बना हुआ है।
वीटीवी के मौसम पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, आज दोपहर में मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्रों में गरज के साथ बारिश जारी रहेगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी वर्षा हो सकती है। वहीं, उत्तरी क्षेत्र के कई प्रांतों और थान्ह होआ से लेकर डाक लक प्रांत के पूर्वी भाग तक गर्म मौसम बना रहेगा।
उत्तरी वियतनाम में, हनोई सहित, मौसम पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार आज पिछले दिनों की तुलना में कम समय तक गर्म मौसम रहेगा, जो मुख्य रूप से दोपहर और शाम के समय रहेगा। दोपहर बाद और शाम को गरज के साथ बारिश होने की संभावना है, जिससे गर्मी से राहत मिलेगी।
इसका कारण यह है कि उत्तरी और उत्तर मध्य वियतनाम को प्रभावित करने वाली शुष्क उत्तर से उत्तर-पश्चिमी हवा धीरे-धीरे कमजोर हो रही है। इसलिए, लाओ काई से होआ बिन्ह, होआ लू, किएन आन और होआन किएम तक के क्षेत्रों में आज दोपहर तापमान 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रहने का अनुमान है। कई क्षेत्रों में दोपहर बाद और शाम को बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है।
मध्य क्षेत्र में, तिन्ह जिया वार्ड ( थान्ह होआ ) से लेकर तुय होआ वार्ड (डाक लक) तक, तापमान 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहता है।
राष्ट्रीय जल-मौसम विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, 13 अगस्त को उत्तरी क्षेत्र ( डिएन बिएन , लाई चाऊ, सोन ला, क्वांग निन्ह और हाई फोंग को छोड़कर) में गर्म मौसम जारी रहेगा, जिसमें अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक हो सकता है; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 60-65% रहेगी।
13 अगस्त को, थान्ह होआ से दा नांग शहर और क्वांग न्गाई के पूर्वी भाग से जिया लाई तक के क्षेत्र में भीषण गर्मी पड़ी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में तो अत्यधिक गर्मी का प्रकोप रहा। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, कुछ स्थानों पर यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक था; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 55-60% थी।
मध्य हाइलैंड्स और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में आज दोपहर और शाम के समय गरज के साथ बारिश होगी, जिससे कुछ इलाकों में 80 मिमी से अधिक भारी बारिश हो सकती है। निचले इलाकों में बाढ़ की आशंका है; पहाड़ी और पर्वतीय क्षेत्रों, विशेष रूप से लाम डोंग प्रांत में भूस्खलन और अचानक बाढ़ का खतरा है।
बारिश से पहले, दोपहर और शाम के समय क्षेत्र में बारी-बारी से धूप और बादल छाए रहे। मध्य उच्चभूमि में तापमान 30 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक नहीं हुआ। दक्षिणी क्षेत्र में तापमान आमतौर पर 31-34 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा।

- उत्तर-पश्चिमी क्षेत्र: शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान; दिन में धूप और गर्मी रहेगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ेगा (डिएन बिएन और लाई चाऊ को छोड़कर)।

VTV.vn - उत्तरी और मध्य वियतनाम में भीषण गर्मी की लहर जारी है, जिससे लगभग 700 स्थानों पर जंगल में आग लगने का खतरा 4 और 5 के स्तर पर है।

आज (12 अगस्त) लाओ काई और फु थो से लेकर पूर्वोत्तर क्षेत्र तक और थान्ह होआ से लेकर ह्यू शहर और दक्षिण मध्य तटीय क्षेत्र तक भीषण गर्मी है। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस है, जबकि कुछ क्षेत्रों में यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक है।
13 अगस्त को उत्तरी क्षेत्र ( डिएन बिएन , लाई चाऊ, सोन ला, क्वांग निन्ह और हाई फोंग को छोड़कर) में गर्म मौसम रहा, जिसमें अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक हो गया; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 60-65% थी।
12-13 अगस्त को थान्ह होआ से दा नांग शहर और क्वांग न्गाई के पूर्वी भाग से जिया लाई तक के क्षेत्र में गर्म मौसम रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा, कुछ स्थानों पर यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 55-60% रहेगी।
उत्तरी वियतनाम में यह व्यापक लू 13 अगस्त तक और मध्य वियतनाम में कम से कम अगले चार दिनों तक जारी रहेगी, जिसके बाद यह धीरे-धीरे कम हो जाएगी।

उत्तरी भाग में भीषण गर्मी का लंबा दौर चल रहा है, जिसमें तुयेन क्वांग देश का सबसे गर्म प्रांत है।
टीपीओ - आज (12 अगस्त) उत्तरी क्षेत्र में भीषण गर्मी जारी है, जहां तापमान 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंचने का अनुमान है और वास्तविक तापमान इससे भी अधिक हो सकता है। यह लू लगभग 14 अगस्त तक जारी रहने की संभावना है। गौरतलब है कि हाल के दिनों में बाक मे (तुयेन क्वांग) लगातार देश का सबसे गर्म प्रांत बना हुआ है, जहां का तापमान अन्य क्षेत्रों की तुलना में कहीं अधिक है।
Báo Tiền Phong•11/08/2026
तुयेन क्वांग प्रांत में स्थित बाक मे कम्यून, जो पहले हा जियांग प्रांत के बाक मे जिले का हिस्सा था, में हाल के दिनों में देश का सबसे अधिक तापमान दर्ज किया गया है, जो 39.5 से 40 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच है।
11 अगस्त को यहां का उच्चतम तापमान 39.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया, जो अन्य स्थानों की तुलना में कहीं अधिक था, जहां आमतौर पर उच्चतम तापमान 37-38 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहता था, जैसे कि हनोई (38 डिग्री), लाओ काई (37.2 डिग्री) और बाक निन्ह (37.3 डिग्री)।
10 अगस्त को बाक मे में तापमान 39 डिग्री सेल्सियस था। 9 अगस्त को वहां का अधिकतम तापमान 39.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया था - जो अन्य स्थानों की तुलना में लगभग 2 डिग्री अधिक था।
आज के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार , उत्तरी क्षेत्र में (लाई चाऊ और डिएन बिएन को छोड़कर) गर्म मौसम जारी रहेगा। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है। न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता लगभग 55-60% रहेगी। बारिश की संभावना कम है और मौसम उमस भरा और गर्म रहेगा।
आज (12 अगस्त) हनोई में गर्म और धूप वाला मौसम रहेगा, कुछ इलाकों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है। दोपहर और शाम के बाद कुछ इलाकों में बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। हवाएं उत्तर-पश्चिम से पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 की गति से चलेंगी। न्यूनतम तापमान 27-29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा। अधिकतम तापमान 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ इलाकों में यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक हो सकता है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
कल (13 अगस्त) उत्तरी क्षेत्र (डिएन बिएन, लाई चाऊ, सोन ला, क्वांग निन्ह और हाई फोंग को छोड़कर) में भीषण गर्मी पड़ने का अनुमान है, जिसमें अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है। 14 अगस्त से उत्तरी क्षेत्र में लू धीरे-धीरे कम होने लगेगी।
थान्ह होआ से लेकर पूर्व फु येन तक , आज धूप खिली रहेगी और गर्मी रहेगी, कुछ इलाकों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है। आज शाम और रात में कुछ इलाकों में बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने, ओले पड़ने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है।
न्यूनतम तापमान 26-29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा। अधिकतम तापमान 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है।
पूर्वानुमान से संकेत मिलता है कि थान्ह होआ से लेकर पूर्व फु येन प्रांत तक के क्षेत्र में लू कई और दिनों तक जारी रहेगी।
दक्षिण मध्य तटीय क्षेत्र में आज धूप खिली रहेगी , शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है। न्यूनतम तापमान 26-29 डिग्री सेल्सियस और अधिकतम तापमान 32-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
मध्य उच्चभूमि में आज सुबह हल्की बारिश होगी, दोपहर और शाम को छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है। न्यूनतम तापमान 20-23 डिग्री सेल्सियस और अधिकतम तापमान 26-29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
दक्षिणी वियतनाम में दिन के समय धूप खिली रहेगी, लेकिन आज शाम और रात में कुछ इलाकों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है, खासकर पूर्वी हिस्से में। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की आशंका है। न्यूनतम तापमान 24-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस और अधिकतम तापमान 32-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
हो ची मिन्ह सिटी में आज धूप खिली रहेगी, शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की आशंका है। न्यूनतम तापमान 24-26 डिग्री सेल्सियस और अधिकतम तापमान 33-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
13-14 अगस्त के मौसम पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में हल्की बारिश होगी। 15 अगस्त से इस क्षेत्र में दोपहर और शाम के समय छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश होगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में मध्यम से भारी बारिश हो सकती है।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी का कहना है कि पूर्वानुमान में बताए गए तापमान और वास्तविक तापमान में 2-4 डिग्री या इससे भी अधिक का अंतर हो सकता है, जो कंक्रीट जैसी सतह की अंतर्निहित स्थितियों, वनस्पति के अनुपात और पानी की मात्रा पर निर्भर करता है।

राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान एवं जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, उत्तरी वियतनाम और थान्ह होआ से ह्यू तक के क्षेत्र में गर्म मौसम जारी रहेगा, कई स्थानों पर भीषण गर्मी रहेगी। हनोई में दिन के दौरान गर्म मौसम बना रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी रहेगी; रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है।
उत्तर-पश्चिमी वियतनाम में गर्म और धूप वाला मौसम रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है, जबकि डिएन बिएन और लाई चाऊ में तापमान कम रहेगा। दोपहर और शाम के समय छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। उत्तर-पूर्वी वियतनाम में भी गर्म और धूप वाला मौसम रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है; दोपहर और शाम के समय छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है।
थान्ह होआ से ह्यू तक, गर्म मौसम जारी है, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ रही है; शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। दक्षिण मध्य तटीय क्षेत्र में धूप खिली रहेगी, उत्तरी भाग में गर्म मौसम रहेगा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी।
इस बीच, मध्य हाइलैंड्स और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में बादल छाए रहेंगे, शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश हो सकती है। दिन के दौरान भी इन क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी। हो ची मिन्ह सिटी में भी मौसम का मिजाज कुछ ऐसा ही रहेगा, शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश हो सकती है।
तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंकों का खतरा रहता है; उत्तरी और मध्य वियतनाम में ओलावृष्टि की संभावना है।
गर्म मौसम और कम आर्द्रता के संयुक्त प्रभाव से, बिजली की खपत बढ़ने के कारण आवासीय क्षेत्रों में आग और विस्फोट का खतरा बढ़ सकता है। लंबे समय तक गर्म मौसम रहने से उच्च तापमान के संपर्क में रहने से निर्जलीकरण भी हो सकता है।
12 अगस्त को विभिन्न क्षेत्रों के लिए मौसम का पूर्वानुमान:
हनोई शहर
न्यूनतम तापमान: 27-29 डिग्री। अधिकतम तापमान: 35-36 डिग्री।
आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे, रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी और गर्मी रहेगी, कुछ इलाकों में भीषण गर्मी होगी। उत्तर-पश्चिम से पश्चिम की ओर हवाएं चलेंगी, जिनकी तीव्रता 2-3 होगी।
उत्तर-पश्चिमी वियतनाम
न्यूनतम तापमान: 25-28 डिग्री सेल्सियस, उत्तर-पश्चिमी क्षेत्र में 23-26 डिग्री सेल्सियस। अधिकतम तापमान: 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस, डिएन बिएन और लाई चाऊ में 32-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस।
शाम और रात में बादल छाए रहेंगे और छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है; दिन में गर्मी और धूप रहेगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में (डिएन बिएन और लाई चाऊ को छोड़कर) अत्यधिक गर्मी पड़ सकती है। हवा हल्की रहेगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवा के झोंके चलने की संभावना है।

12 अगस्त, 2026 के लिए मौसम पूर्वानुमान: उत्तरी वियतनाम में भीषण गर्मी जारी रहेगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में तापमान 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक रहेगा और शाम को गरज के साथ बारिश की संभावना है। मध्य वियतनाम में भी भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी। मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में शाम को कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी बारिश होगी।
VietNamNet•11/08/2026
राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान एवं जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, उत्तरी वियतनाम में लू की तीव्रता में थोड़ी कमी आ रही है और धीरे-धीरे इसका क्षेत्रफल भी कम हो रहा है। 12 अगस्त को लू उत्तरी वियतनाम के मध्य और निचले इलाकों में केंद्रित रहेगी, जहां अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा।
मध्य वियतनाम में लू की लहर तेज हो रही है और धीरे-धीरे दक्षिण की ओर फैल रही है; 12 अगस्त से, सबसे गर्म क्षेत्र संभवतः ह्यू, दा नांग, क्वांग न्गाई, जिया लाई और डैक लक प्रांतों और शहरों के तटीय क्षेत्रों में केंद्रित होंगे।
विशेष रूप से, 12 अगस्त को हनोई में मौसम गर्म और बेहद गर्म था, मध्य क्षेत्र में अधिकतम तापमान 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया, और कुछ स्थानों पर तो यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक था; जबकि उत्तरी, दक्षिणी और पश्चिमी क्षेत्रों में तापमान 34-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा।
14 अगस्त से उत्तरी क्षेत्र में लू की लहर धीरे-धीरे कम होने की उम्मीद है, लेकिन मध्य क्षेत्र में यह जारी रह सकती है।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी सलाह देती है कि लू के दौरान, लोगों को दोपहर और दोपहर बाद के शुरुआती समय के बीच (जब गर्मी सबसे तीव्र होती है) बाहरी गतिविधियों को कम से कम करना चाहिए।
विशेष रूप से, सतह की स्थितियों (कंक्रीट, डामर) और आर्द्रता के आधार पर, वास्तविक रूप से महसूस किया गया बाहरी तापमान पूर्वानुमानित तापमान से 2-4 डिग्री अधिक हो सकता है।
इस बीच, 12 अगस्त को मध्य हाइलैंड्स, पूर्वी लाम डोंग प्रांत और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में दिन और रात दोनों समय बारिश और छिटपुट गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, जिनमें 10-30 मिमी तक वर्षा हो सकती है। कुछ क्षेत्रों में 70 मिमी से अधिक भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है (बारिश दोपहर और रात में केंद्रित रहेगी)। गरज के साथ बौछारों के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवा के झोंके चलने की संभावना है।
देश के सभी क्षेत्रों के लिए 12 अगस्त, 2026 का मौसम पूर्वानुमान:

Britain, already infamous for its notorious weather, now faces a new reality: a summer that’s just too hot, even for the British sense of understatement. Per the BBC, the Met Office says summer 2026 is racing toward becoming the country's hottest on record. Between June 1 and August 10, the mean UK temperature has hit 16.48°C, which is 1.88°C above the recent 30-year average. If August simply stays average, this year will eclipse the record set just last year.
Safe to say that weather records are tumbling fast. For the first time, the UK has seen May, June, and July temperatures all hit or exceed 35°C in one season. By July, the nation endured eight separate days topping 34°C, which is a new record, outpacing the infamous heatwaves of 1976 and 2020.
But heat, as always, is not equal. Per Sky News, some cities bear the brunt more than other places. Layers of concrete, glass, tarmac, and high-rises, not to mention millions of engines and appliances, trap warmth after sunset, making urban nights restless and sticky. Microclimates mean two neighbourhoods in the same city can experience wildly different temperatures. The Met Office notes that urbanisation is amplifying these emerging risks.
Here, we jot down a list of Britain’s urban hotspots, where the heat hits the hardest.
The capital of Britain holds the crown for urban heat. Its sheer density, endless rows of terraced housing, and minimal green space leave entire boroughs exposed. London reached a mind-boggling 40°C in the 2022 heatwave, leading to hundreds of heat-related deaths. City Hall has mapped extreme heat risk, highlighting neighborhoods where the lack of trees and open space leaves residents sweltering.
England’s second city stands out for its vulnerability. Extensive research from the University of Birmingham pinpoints central and eastern districts, where dense housing combines with little parkland and higher levels of deprivation. A recent Sky analysis, in fact, found Birmingham had more at-risk communities than any other city under review.
The “rain city” of England now faces hotter summers. Manchester’s heat island is well studied, and researchers have tracked its intensifying trend. Loss of urban green space, replaced by new buildings, directly drives the effect, transforming a grey, drizzly image into something noticeably less comfortable.
2022 saw Leeds break 40°C. Data shows inner-city Leeds gets much hotter than nearby rural areas, sometimes by as much as 8°C. The worst-affected neighborhoods, unsurprisingly, tend to be poorer, making heat as much a question of social justice as meteorology.
Regularly flagged by urban climate studies, Nottingham’s blend of compact living, heavy construction, and socio-economic vulnerability marks it as a city where summer heat is increasingly dangerous.
As a major port city, Liverpool isn’t immune. Researchers here are exploring how residents experience urban heat and what local authorities can do. The answer? Local context matters far more than official thermometers alone.
Like many post-industrial English cities, Leicester’s problem is dense, near-treeless urban neighborhoods that bake in the heat. City-wide averages hide the fact that people in these dense pockets get exposed to much higher temperatures, which is a challenge for city planning.
The city’s hilly, green outskirts offer some protection, but central Sheffield is just as susceptible as the other big players. Vulnerable residents in poorly ventilated flats face the greatest risks when hot spells drag on.
With a fast-growing population and limited green relief downtown, Bristol is another city where heat is becoming a major concern. The danger isn’t just outside; it’s how nighttime heat builds in homes, endangering the elderly and those with health conditions.
Historically spared the worst, northern England is no longer out of the woods. Newcastle’s cooler climate isn’t a guarantee against risk, as the relentless baseline warming means local health and housing authorities have to adapt.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government understood firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather.
This week's latest heatwave comes as more areas in England were placed under drought status on Monday and firefighters continue to battle a significant wildfire in the New Forest in Hampshire.
The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning, external for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible
It comes as the record for the number of days reaching 30C in any year in the UK has been broken, according to the Met Office, with Sunday the 35th day of the year so far.
The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.
It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June.
A spokesperson for No 10 said this summer was proving "challenging" in the UK, particularly for "firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units".
"We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment," they said.
The hottest weather this week is expected on Thursday across the Midlands, Eastern England, London and south-east England, Yorkshire and Humber.
Temperatures could potentially reach 38C which would equal the highest temperature of the summer so far recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on 26 June.
This would be the hottest August day since 2003, when 38.5C was recorded.
It is also likely to be the fourth calendar month this year to record 35C or more, which is unprecedented.
On Monday, drought officials declared 71.3% of England in drought, meaning there are a total of 45 million people now living in a drought area, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.
Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August, and 458 in July, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.
A fire in the New Forest has been burning since Sunday, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood.
Last week, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS should be "preparing for summer pressures now in the same way we prepare for winter".
She told LBC Radio plans were in place to respond to higher numbers of people coming in to A&E.
On Tuesday, the Met Office said this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, with the mean temperature currently at 16.48C set to surpass the figure set just last year.
This is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the Cobra meeting was just a first step, and a "climate emergency" had led to hundreds of deaths and was "stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit".
He called for "concrete action" and said he looked forward to hearing how Burnham intended to "prepare for the threats to come".
Amber heat health alerts also in force
The UK's Health Security Agency has also issued amber heat health alerts, which cover the whole of England.
Heat health alerts warn the public and medical professionals when periods of hot or cold weather pose a threat to health.
They warn that significant impacts are likely across social and health care, including a rise in deaths.
The alerts are in place until Friday evening.
When will the heatwave end?
This heatwave should be shorter lived than others so far this summer with temperatures starting to feel noticeably cooler over the weekend.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will not experience the same extreme heat as southern England, although eastern parts of Northern Ireland, southern and eastern Scotland will still see temperatures well above the heatwave threshold.
They will be notably above average for mid-August and the humidity is likely to intensify on Wednesday night into Thursday.
Some places could reach the mid to high 20s Celsius on Wednesday - when a typical August daytime temperature would generally be in the high teens to low 20s.
Western Scotland and western parts of Northern Ireland are likely to remain somewhat cooler due to cloud and occasional rain moving in from the Atlantic.
While confidence in the details remains low, this could open the door for showers and perhaps some prolonged spells of rain.
To alleviate drought though, months of above-average rainfall is needed.
What has caused the summer heat?
The persistence of high-pressure weather systems over recent months has been unusual but this is the type of summer scientists have warned about due to climate change.
As average temperatures rise – mainly due to the burning of fossil fuels around the world – hot weather becomes much more likely and more intense.
While temperatures will continue to vary from year to year, scientists warn that summers will keep getting hotter on average as carbon emissions continue to heat up the planet.
This means future heatwaves will be able to reach even higher temperatures than the same weather systems of the past.

Heatwave helps garden plant 'go bananas'
A banana plant in a woman's garden has produced 24 pieces of fruit due to the hot weather.
Cathy Neville, from Seaton, near Looe in Cornwall, said she had been "really surprised" when the 11ft-high (3.35m) plant she was given as a gift seven year's ago had "gone bananas".
The Eden Project's director of horticulture, Peter Jones, said: "Although banana plants can thrive in this part of the country, it is very unusual to have one that produces fruit."
Guy Barter, from the Royal Horticultural Society, said bananas never used to flower 20 years ago in the UK and attributed Neville's fruit to the climate having become warmer.
Neville said the plant was "tiny" when she planted it.
"I just kept emptying the ash from our fire, because they like potash, and mulching the base of it, and they've just gone bananas," she continued.
"I was really surprised, I knew it could happen but I know it's unusual. It's fantastic to see the plant doing what it's supposed to do.
"It's quite an impressive flower, I've never seen one before, it looks a bit like a coconut.
"It's quite a damp valley that we live in so there's a lot of moisture in the air that will help them to grow."
Neville, who has had horticulture training at Kew Gardens in London and is a member of a gardening group, said she did not think there was a recorded case in the UK of people being able to grow bananas to eat, except perhaps in a biome.
Barter said heat-loving plants such as olives, figs and apricots were also excelling as temperatures rose, while traditional British crops like gooseberries and rhubarb were declining in some areas.
"The climate is getting warmer and bananas never used to flower 20 years ago," he said.

“If it is 35C outdoors, I can get the temperature down to 21C,” says Andrew Ingram of the sanctuary that his living room has provided this summer.
“On the nights I’ve slept in there, you have to put your thick pyjamas on,” jokes Ingram, who lives in Maidenhead, Berkshire, with his wife, Sue.
“When I post on Facebook about it, people say: ‘That’s air conditioning’ and I say: ‘No, it’s the heat pump.’ It’s just working the other way around.”
Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, a heat pump transfers heat energy from one place to another. However, despite the name, heat pumps can be used for cooling, too.
The energy is released through an “emitter” such as a radiator or underfloor heating. The Ingrams have an air source heat pump. It extracts heat from the air outside and uses it to warm the radiators of their three-bedroom house (this is called an air-to-water system).
In 2023, when the Ingrams ripped out their gas boiler, the firm suggested they consider whether they wanted to cool any rooms.
“We thought about it because the sitting room gets really hot, and that’s the room we spend time in,” Ingram says.
“It’s been a revelation. We bought it on the basis that there might be a heatwave, and it’s been an absolute lifeline this year.
“You know those times when you are really feeling exhausted and want to sit somewhere cool. We turn it right down and then let the temperature drift back up again.”
The couple have radiators throughout but the living room also has another “emitter” – called a fan coil unit. This is an appliance that blows air over hot or cold pipes. The whole new home energy system cost roughly £18,600, with the cooling aspect accounting for £1,700 of that.
“If you’re pumping cool water around a property, it’s a bit like putting cool beer in a glass on a warm day,” says Ingram of what is potentially one of the pitfalls of cooling this way.
“You get loads of condensation, so you either have to wrap pipes in quite sophisticated trunking or do what we did, which is have them outside.
“We used the cooling a bit in 2024, and, guess what, in 2025 even more – and in 2026 we’ve been a rather popular place for people to visit.”
The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to assist homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water system (a heat pump that extracts heat from the ground through buried pipes).
Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000.
If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get an interest-free loan or a grant to make your home more energy efficient.
To qualify for funding, the heat pump must be certified through the Microgeneration Certification Scheme, which certifies installers.
Previously heat pumps that also cooled required planning permission, as the permitted development rights rules (legal permissions that allow certain home improvements without a planning application) stated they had to be solely for heating. The PDR has now been updated to allow cooling.
To date, Britons have mostly installed air-to-water systems, and of the UK’s 358,000 heat pumps, approximately 323,000 are this type, according to MCS data.
This could be about to change because the government is to offer £2,500 grants for air conditioning units that can heat and cool. The air-to-air heat pumps move heat using wall-mounted fans and cost about £4,500 to fit in a flat or small house. (Air-to-water heat pumps typically cost in the region of £12,000.)
The run of heatwaves has thrown the spotlight on “heat-trap homes”. A recent report by the Climate Change Committee said that hotter heatwaves could lead to 92% of existing homes overheating by 2050 and they may require air conditioning, as passive measures such as drawing curtains and opening windows are unlikely to be enough.
A recent study conducted in the Energy House 2.0 – a £16m climate-controlled chamber at the University of Salford – found that using a heat pump for cooling can “significantly reduce overheating” in modern homes.
Two new modern houses have been built inside the weather simulation facility so that scientists can test how “real” homes perform under extreme conditions.
The Salford scientists paired a heat pump with fan coils in one of the houses. When the lab weather was 32C, the rooms stayed comfortable – between 19C and 24.9C. With the heat pump running around the clock, the cost was £2.50-£3 a day.
Prof Lubo Jankovic, the scientist leading the research, says the results “demonstrate that reversible heat pumps can play an important role in protecting future homes against overheating”.
But Jankovic says the challenge of designing systems with both heating and cooling in mind “needs to be addressed before cooling this way becomes mainstream”.
With the October price cap predicted to exceed £1,700 a year for a typical dual fuel bill, the big question for many is: will a heat pump save me money?
A recent poll by the consumer group Which? revealed growing consumer interest in heat pumps, but also that they were a “high-stakes gamble” owing to their unfamiliarity, high upfront costs and uncertain impact on bills.
One way to get a better understanding is to look round a home with one and quiz the owner. The charity Nesta runs the “visit a heat pump” scheme, which offers tours of more than 1,200 homes, including the Ingrams’.
When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.
The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits.
Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can save about £330 a year compared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.
The Ingrams have solar panels and a home battery to help keep their bills down. “There’s lots of juice in the batteries from the solar,” Ingram says. “The batteries charge up overnight if they’re not full, but they have been recently. So if you want to run the pump, it is running on free or very cheap electricity.”

As temperatures rise, workers are losing working hours and income while facing growing risks of heat exhaustion, kidney disease and other health problems. Researchers estimate the wage losses amount to nearly 1.4% of Bangladesh’s GDP.
Amina Begum, 44, spends her working day moving from one home to another in Dhaka, cleaning, cooking and doing other household chores. As a temporary domestic worker, she works in five homes before returning to her small room in Kallyanpur slum.
Five years ago, Amina came to Dhaka from Nilphamari in northern Bangladesh after erosion along the Teesta River destroyed her family’s home. Having escaped one climate-related hardship, she now faces another in the capital: extreme heat.
Amina shares a small tin-roofed room with three other women. There is no fan and no gas connection, so they cook on a traditional stove inside the cramped space. The metal roof absorbs heat throughout the day, while cooking adds more heat inside.
By the time Amina finishes cooking, her clothes are often soaked with sweat. She feels exhausted and sleepy, but there is little opportunity to rest.
At the end of every month, she has rent to pay and elderly, sick parents back home who depend on her financial support. Even when the heat leaves her exhausted, stopping work is not an option.
Amina’s experience is far from isolated. For millions of informal workers in Bangladesh, rising temperatures are increasingly becoming both a health and livelihood crisis.
A new study estimates that extreme heat and its long-term health consequences cost Bangladesh’s informal workers about $6.22 billion in lost wages every year, equivalent to 1.38% of the country’s GDP.
The study was jointly conducted by the UK-based International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) and the Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP). Titled No escaping the heat: Health and economic impacts of heat
stress on informal workers in urban Bangladesh, the study is scheduled to be published tomorrow, Wednesday.
Researchers surveyed 175 informal-worker households in Dhaka. Of them, 122 were primarily engaged in outdoor occupations, including construction, road work and rickshaw pulling, while 53 were associated with indoor work, primarily garment manufacturing. The research also included observations of work and rest patterns, focus group discussions, interviews, household case studies and medical review of health findings.
The findings carry national significance in a country where informal employment accounts for 84.9% of total employment. For many of these workers, income depends directly on their ability to show up and remain productive each day. When heat forces them to stop or slow down, their earnings fall with their physical capacity.
Twelve Hours in Winter, Five or Six in Summer
Amina mainly works indoors. Across the city, Azizul Islam faces the same heat from an entirely different workplace.
Azizul is a rickshaw puller living in Korail, one of Dhaka’s largest informal settlements. He moved to the capital from the coastal district of Satkhira after climate-related pressures forced him to leave his home.
During the cooler winter months, Azizul can pull his rickshaw for as long as 12 hours a day. In summer, however, extreme heat often limits him to five or six hours, sometimes even less.
Fewer hours on the road mean fewer passengers and less income.
Azizul says he frequently becomes extremely tired during hot weather and has suffered from diarrhea several times. On some days, he becomes too weak to continue working.
There is no paid sick leave for a worker like Azizul. If he cannot work, he does not earn. During the hottest months, the repeated loss of working hours reduces his monthly income and sometimes leaves him unable to contribute as much as usual to his family.
The study found a similar pattern across the workers surveyed. An outdoor worker loses an average of 23.7 working days a year because of heat, compared with 13.5 days for an indoor worker. The corresponding annual wage losses average $148.86 for outdoor workers and $89.10 for indoor workers.
Heat Pushes Workers Further Below a Living Wage
Those losses are being absorbed by households already struggling to earn enough to meet basic needs.
Using a living-wage benchmark for Dhaka of Tk 30,459 per month, researchers found that outdoor-worker households earn 41.4% below a living wage, while indoor-worker households fall 33.8% short.
Once heat-related wage losses are included, the gaps widen to 46.4% for outdoor-worker households and 36.8% for indoor-worker households.
In effect, heat is taking income away from people who already earn substantially less than what researchers estimate they need for a basic but decent standard of living.
An ‘Invisible’ $6.22 Billion Loss
At the national level, researchers estimate that the immediate effects of extreme heat result in around 1.18 billion lost workdays annually, costing workers about $4.10 billion in wages, equivalent to 0.91% of GDP.
The researchers separately estimate that chronic kidney disease associated with long-term heat exposure could result in another roughly 610 million lost workdays and $2.12 billion in annual wage losses.
Together, the immediate and long-term losses amount to approximately 1.79 billion workdays and $6.22 billion in wages, or 1.38% of GDP.
Even that figure is conservative, according to the study. It covers wage losses among informal workers engaged in physically demanding occupations but excludes losses among formal workers, healthcare expenses, supply-chain disruption, production losses and other indirect economic effects.
Ritu Bharadwaj, director of climate resilience, finance and loss and damage at IIED, said one reason such a large economic burden receives limited policy attention is that the damage is largely invisible.
Unlike a destroyed road or ruined crop, income lost because of reduced working capacity leaves no physical trace. A rickshaw puller who stops during the hottest hours or a garment worker who slows down on an overheated production line absorbs the loss through forgone earnings, depleted savings or debt.
“It is real loss and damage, but it does not appear in any official assessment, so policymakers never see the aggregate,” Bharadwaj said.
She said expressing the losses as a share of GDP and connecting them with critical sectors such as construction, transport and manufacturing could shift the discussion from welfare to productivity and economic growth.
The study similarly notes that workers experiencing these losses are concentrated in sectors that underpin wider economic activity, meaning the consequences extend beyond individual households.
Indoor Workers Are Not Safe From Heat
The risks facing someone like Azizul, who works under the sun, may be obvious. But the research challenges the assumption that working indoors provides substantial protection from extreme heat.
During the hot season, 66.4% of outdoor workers and 66% of indoor workers met the clinical threshold for heat exhaustion, Bharadwaj said. The study also found that about one in three outdoor workers and one in seven indoor workers reached the threshold for heatstroke.
Garment workers may receive little direct sunlight, but many spend long shifts in enclosed workplaces where heat accumulates from machinery, ironing and pressing, crowded production floors and inadequate ventilation.
Bharadwaj said workers averaged just 1.6 breaks a day. Some workers also restricted their water intake because toilet breaks were limited, increasing their risk of dehydration.
And exposure does not necessarily end when a shift does.
Among the households surveyed, 66% of indoor-worker households and 54.1% of outdoor-worker households lived under tin or asbestos roofs. The research also found severe overcrowding: 92.9% of indoor-worker households and 57.3% of outdoor-worker households fell below the study’s minimum living-space benchmark.
“The heat does not end at the factory gate either,” Bharadwaj said.
The report says hot and overcrowded homes, poor ventilation, unreliable water and frequent power cuts can leave workers with little opportunity to rest and physically recover before returning to work the next day.
Because Bangladesh’s garment sector produces for global brands, Bharadwaj said international buyers also have a responsibility to address workers’ heat exposure.
She said enforceable temperature thresholds, adequate ventilation, drinking water and protected rest breaks should be incorporated into sourcing and auditing requirements in much the same way fire and building safety have been addressed, with protections extending down the supply chain.
“Buyers benefit from this workforce,” Bharadwaj said, “and they are well placed to help fund and enforce the conditions that keep it safe and productive.”
The Risk of Permanent Kidney Damage
The consequences of extreme heat may extend far beyond temporary exhaustion or a few lost hours of work.
Dr. Nihar Ranjan Das, a medicine specialist at Alliance Hospital Ltd., said workers often sweat heavily in extreme heat but do not drink enough water. Many also do not get adequate breaks at work or sufficient sleep after returning home.
The combination can increase the risk of dehydration, fatigue and other health complications, including kidney problems, he said.
Low incomes compound the problem. Das said many workers do not undergo regular medical checkups even when they become ill because they cannot afford the expense or fear losing income by taking time away from work.
“Poverty and extreme heat are silently harming these workers,” Das said. “Yet they are an important driving force of our economy. We need to pay much greater attention to their health.”
He said the government could expand awareness programs on heat-related health risks, while companies, NGOs and international development organizations could help improve access to safe drinking water, adequate rest, medical checkups and better living conditions.
The study’s findings point to potentially serious long-term consequences.
Researchers found that 23.1% of workers reported symptoms consistent with acute kidney injury. They estimate that around 6% approximately one in every 17 workers could eventually develop chronic kidney disease as a consequence of repeated heat exposure and dehydration.
Scaled to the national informal workforce engaged in high-physical-labour occupations, the researchers estimate that about 3.56 million workers could develop CKD as a long-term consequence of heat exposure.
The resulting reduction in working capacity could account for approximately 609.7 million lost workdays and $2.12 billion in annual wage losses.
Bharadwaj said the damage can be permanent and may emerge years after the initial exposure, making it difficult to trace back to workplace heat.
No Enforceable Safe Heat Limit
The study also identifies major gaps in Bangladesh’s existing worker protections.
The Bangladesh Labour Act 2006 and Labour Rules 2015 require employers to provide drinking water, adequate ventilation, tolerable workplace temperatures, rest rooms and first aid. But there is no specific temperature threshold above which working conditions are legally considered unsafe.
The Bangladesh Meteorological Department issues heat alerts, but those warnings do not create a legal obligation for employers to take specific action.
Coverage is another problem. Many protections depend on the number of workers employed at an establishment, meaning small workplaces, outdoor worksites and much of the informal economy fall outside their reach.
Heatstroke, heat exhaustion and heat-related kidney disease are also not currently included among the occupational diseases covered by the relevant provisions identified in the report.
Researchers recommend introducing enforceable heat thresholds based on wet-bulb globe temperature, or WBGT. Crossing the threshold would trigger mandatory protections such as drinking water, electrolytes, shaded rest areas and adjusted working hours, with outdoor work suspended at higher levels.
They also recommend recognizing heatstroke, heat exhaustion and heat-related kidney disease as occupational diseases and replacing workplace-size thresholds with a hazard-based approach, so protection depends on heat exposure rather than how many people an establishment employs.
Protection Would Cost a Fraction of the Losses
Protecting such a large workforce would require money. But the researchers argue that failing to act is already costing far more.
They propose heat-triggered cash assistance for workers whose earnings are disrupted by dangerous temperatures.
The cash-transfer component would cost an estimated $31.3 million in a normal year, $62.5 million in a hot year and $93.8 million in a record year.
When interim health support and improved access to food programs are added, the overall package would cost about $69.8 million in a normal year, $101 million in a hot year and $132.3 million in a record year.
Much of the infrastructure needed to deliver the assistance already exists, the researchers argue.
Payments could be distributed through mobile financial services such as bKash and Nagad, recipients targeted through the National ID system and support triggered by Bangladesh Meteorological Department heat alerts. Bangladesh also has experience with forecast-based anticipatory cash transfers.
“The point is that this cost is already being paid,” Bharadwaj said. “It is being paid invisibly, by workers, in lost wages, medical bills and permanent damage to their health, rather than visibly through the budget.”
Evidence reviewed by the researchers from eight countries, including Bangladesh, found that every $1 invested in anticipatory action generated an estimated $2.06 to $5.17 in avoided losses and development gains.
Bharadwaj said international climate finance should ultimately help fund such protection. But workers should not have to continue absorbing the losses while governments negotiate over international funding.
The report proposes a layered approach: direct public funding to cover recurring losses during normal and severe heat seasons, with parametric insurance or similar risk-sharing mechanisms used for exceptional years when costs spike.
Workers Are Already Paying the Price
Amina does not calculate the heat in billions of dollars or fractions of GDP.
Her calculation is simpler: how many homes she can work in that day, how much her body can endure, whether she can pay her rent at the end of the month and how much money will remain to send to her parents.
For Azizul, the calculation is much the same. In winter, his body allows him to pull a rickshaw for as long as 12 hours. In extreme summer heat, it may force him off the road after five or six.
Different jobs, different parts of Dhaka, but the economic equation is the same: when their bodies can no longer tolerate the heat, their income stops.
The researchers argue that protecting workers from heat should therefore be viewed not simply as a welfare expense, but as an investment in livelihoods, public health, productivity and economic growth.

The UK's fourth heatwave of 2026 has triggered a government Cobra emergency meeting and broken a 31-year national record, arriving into an insurance market already struggling under the weight of record subsidence claims, accelerating wildfire incidents, and a forecast underwriting loss for the year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will chair a Cobra committee meeting on Wednesday to coordinate the government's response to the extreme heat, according to the BBC. Temperatures are expected to peak in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, with the Met Office issuing a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, when 38C is possible.
The BBC reports that the record for the number of days reaching 30C in any year has been broken, with 35 days now exceeding that threshold - surpassing the previous record of 34 days set in 1995. The Met Office has also issued amber heat health alerts across the whole of England, warning of significant impacts across health and social care, including a rise in deaths.
For insurers and brokers, this is not a background weather story. It is the latest pressure point in what the data already suggests is shaping up to be one of the most costly years for UK property claims on record.
According to the Association of British Insurers (ABI), subsidence claims totalled £153 million in the first half of 2026 alone, supporting close to 9,000 households. The average settled subsidence claim reached £17,820 in the first quarter of 2026 - the highest figure on record, up 9% year-on-year from £16,295 - following 2025 payouts that hit a record £307 million.
Writing in May 2026 following that month's heatwave, Steven Coxon, head of subsidence at Claims Consortium Group, warned that ground conditions were already significantly damaged from the previous year's severe weather.
"Since 2018 we have had three surge events - 2018, 2022 and 2025 - and based on current MORECS data there is the potential for us to see yet another surge event this year," he said. "The ground at the start of 2026 was still significantly damaged because of the severe weather conditions in 2025, and due to continued dry/hot weather in 2026, we are tracking a very similar picture to that of 2025."
A fourth heatwave, arriving in August, compounds that position further still. Clay-rich soils across much of England shrink as they dry out, cracking foundations, walls and driveways. With soil moisture deficits already elevated before this week's temperatures arrive, the conditions for another surge year are in place.
Wildfire is adding a second line of exposure. The Environment Agency has recorded 110 wildfires on Sites of Special Scientific Interest in 2026, and a New Forest heathland fire earlier this week illustrated how a single incident can generate simultaneous motor, property and business interruption claims. Many standard UK property policies were not drafted with wildfire as a named peril, leaving clients who assume coverage with potential gaps that a broker can close before a loss event, not after.
The drought dimension extends the exposure further still. The Environment Agency confirmed in late July that seven areas of England - covering just over half the country - are officially in drought, including London, East Anglia, Hampshire, and the whole of south-west England. For farm insurers, reduced grass growth and lower crop yields are already features of the season, with the National Farmers' Union warning members to prepare for conditions extending well into the year.
The financial backdrop makes the stakes for brokers concrete. Deloitte has forecast that UK home insurers will swing to a net underwriting loss in 2026, with the combined ratio projected to reach 102.1% as storm, flood, and subsidence claims accumulate. UK property insurance payouts reached a record £6.1 billion in 2025, according to ABI data, with weather-related claims up 14% year-on-year.
The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) launched its General Insurance Stress Test in May 2026 specifically to press firms on climate-driven property exposure - a regulatory signal that wildfire and heat-related risk are moving from the periphery of underwriting toward the centre. A market under that kind of financial pressure is more likely to tighten terms and scrutinise exposed risks at renewal.
The practical implication for brokers is a narrowing window. Clients in clay-soil regions, rural areas, agricultural land, or properties near heathland carry compounding exposure across subsidence, wildfire and drought. Reviewing excess structures, checking whether wildfire is named or excluded in property wordings, and assessing motor policies for clients operating near heathland in dry periods are all steps that remain available before the next renewal cycle, rather than after a claim makes the gap visible.
The BBC reports that while this heatwave should be shorter-lived than others so far this summer, temperatures will remain notably above average into the weekend, and months of above-average rainfall would be needed to alleviate the drought conditions already in place.

There’s a running theme on NXT the past few weeks: The men are kinda meh and need an infusion. Now, I’m not sure how smart it is to repeatedly tell the audience that the people competing on your wrestling program aren’t up to snuff as it bakes in the idea that they’re not worth one’s time. Sure, Grayson Waller is a heel who can and should say anything to get under everyone’s skin. But when everyone reacts to it in a way that validates his message, that’s where it gets murky for me. Especially when it comes at the cost of other matches, like when Saquan Sugars and Dion Lennox interrupted Wren Sinclair vs. Zaria with their drama all because Grayson got in Saquan’s face about stepping up. The irony of the men interrupting a women’s match isn’t lost on me either.
However, the call to action on the men’s side opens the door for something different. On one hand, there’s Waller, and there’s Zilla Fatu on the other.
Zilla cooled off NXT’s Heatwave plans. He wrecked the main event between Grayson and Cruz Santana when he attacked Cruz. Now, that should result in a Cruz win since that would disqualify Grayson. But NXT always plays fast and loose with established wrestling rules for the sake of story. That aside, Zilla’s entrance was the most exciting moment of the night, and possibly an even bigger indictment on the men’s locker room:
There’s no one or nothing exciting about NXT men’s division. Look no further than Tony D’Angelo’s commentary during the main event. I like Tony D a lot. But they put the man on the announce table and he added nothing. He sounded monotone, flat, and showed very little character. Even worse, most of what he said came out of pro wrestling cliche 101.
And because NXT is mostly men, that makes the product overall uninspiring. Zilla has eyes on Tony’s gold. Guess what? That’s the storyline for basically everyone in NXT. I know, I know: Pro wrestling is a pre-determined sport built on wins and losses. Championship gold should be everyone’s goal. But there are barely any stories not about a championship. More to that point, NXT is reheating the same stories and templates on a yearly basis now. The faces change but the ideas remain the same: Get a bunch of people in the ring together, make them say “opportunity” a dozen times, design a few matches around one or two of them earning a title shot. Rinse and repeat. That framework is even more pronounced now with a GM finding his footing and a locker room hellbent on proving an Aussie wrong.
Zilla won’t cure what ails the men’s locker room because those issues are systemic. He’s a band-aid at best; something to stop the bleeding on a show that desperately needs a new direction. The wrestling is still solid in spots but at this point, NXT is so far removed from its heyday that it might be hard for someone new to comprehend that Black and Gold Era existed.
It’s not even near the NXT 2.0 days.
B-Sides
- No Shawn Spears? No problem. EK Prosper filled in for the Chairman as Lizzy Rain’s partner against Izzi Dame & Niko Vance. Why? Because of the continued storyline about the men needing to step the F up. EK’s initiative paid off later as Rey Mysterio chose him to dance with La Parka and two other wrestlers for a shot at Rey Fenix’s AAA Cruiserweight Championship. The brief opening match pushed Lizzy’s beef with what’s left of The Culling forward while segueing to the territory putting EK in a good position. It didn’t standout but it accomplished its goals. Which is a highlight for NXT these days.
- Dion and Saquan are still battling. I understand the DarkState fallout needs to be a big deal, but it’s still going weeks later with no real forward movement. Saquan is still battling an entire crew with nothing or nobody by his side but a baseball bat. DarkState is still supposedly ready to dominate again but have to use three people to defeat one.
- Wren Sinclair had Zaria beat. Possibly. Dion and Saquan showed up like the Road Runner and Wil E. Coyote, threw off her mojo, and Zaria got the W. That set the stage for a rematch at Heatwave in a title unification match. That’s right, NXT is getting rid of the Women’s Speed Championship. That’s probably a smart move at this point.
- Speaking of Speed titles, Lucien Price’s victory over Lexis King this week earned him a Speed Championship match. Lucien chopped that man so hard that his chest bled. How is that even possible? Lucien is a heavy hitter who is finally getting some character. BirthRight keeps looking like an experiment gone wrong. And I think that’s partially because Lexis is the front man. No diss to him at all but leading a crew, specifically this crew, isn’t his forte.
- Despite my feelings on NXT overall, Mason Rook keeps shining. He does things a person his size shouldn’t do, like a freaking Enziguri. Kam Hendrix defeated my favorite big man through chicanery a la an exposed turnbuckle. That means this war between he and Kam is nowhere near finished.
NXT is a messy show right now. As we said in the Cageside offices, it’s pretty much the same show every week. It relies on a surprise finish for excitement rathe than interesting storytelling. The matches are fine but stay at that level because they aren’t doing much work between matches to make me care about the wrestlers in the match. If everyone’s sole motivation is “I want my opportunity” then that leads to a bland show all around. NXT has a variety of wrestlers. Shiloh Hill is not like Jackson Drake. What it needs is a variety of stories in which to make the wrestlers flourish.
What say you, Cagesiders?

Would you buy a cauliflower that looks like it's been sunburnt or a cucumber that's curled back on itself?
Farmers across the UK are grappling with one of the driest, hottest growing seasons in decades. Repeated heatwaves after a warmer than usual spring have led to predictions of the worst harvest since records began.
The heat is not only affecting how much produce is grown, but also how it looks.
Retailers usually reject fruit and vegetables that don't meet strict guidelines on size, shape and colour. But with supplies under pressure, many are now expected to loosen those rules rather than risk empty shelves.
That means shoppers could start seeing smaller, wonkier or oddly coloured veg on the shelves in the coming weeks - and sellers and growers say it's still good to eat.
'Sun-tanned' cauliflowers
Cauliflower is one of the most affected vegetables in hot weather because it needs lots of water.
Its heads are usually shielded from sunlight by the leaves, but in this year more light is reaching them and turning them yellow.
Emilie Vanpoperinghe, co-founder of Oddbox, a subscription company that sells surplus produce that supermarkets reject, said it is "purely a cosmetic defect" and the plants taste exactly the same.
She said Oddbox acquired 6,000 cauliflower heads last week that were too dark for supermarkets to sell.
Growers are reporting that their water reserves are depleted, Vanpoperinghe said, which means the cauliflower and broccoli family of brassicas will experience slower growth, leading to shorter supplies.
That short supply means retailers may soon start stocking "sun-tanned" cauliflower because "their biggest nightmare is empty shelves", she said. "They want to make sure that they've got availability of produce all the time."
Curly cucumbers
Growers are also reporting cucumbers that are coming out misshapen, with some bending back into a spiral.
That is because the plants are grown in greenhouses which overheat in the high outdoor temperatures, causing the plants to become stressed, Vanpoperingh said.
"Even if they get the irrigation then it's just extreme heat, which means the plant is not able to grow anymore."
Holey pak choi
John Harper, a farmer in Worcestershire, grows pak choi for Sainsbury's, Aldi and Co-op, and has discarded more produce than usual this year because of tiny holes made by pests.
Flea beetles thrive in hot, dry conditions, and farmers are no longer allowed to use as many pesticides as before, meaning net covers are Harper's only defence.
Supermarkets' strict cosmetic rules mean "one tiny little hole can render the plant useless", he said, but some have temporarily loosened the rules.
"We've been working with them through this hot period and in general they sort of get it," he added.
Harper said the vast majority of affected pak choi is still edible - even if "it seems to be quite tasty" for the beetles too.
Knobbly potatoes
Lucy Munns, a potato farmer in Cambridgeshire, said the hot weather will stunt the root vegetable's growth, leading to oddly shaped tubers that supermarkets and chip shops, which she supplies, wouldn't normally buy.
When the weather gets cooler after a hot period, instead of the main potato tuber growing "it tends to grow a little knobble on the end".
"Trying to find people that will accept potatoes like that is very difficult. So that ultimately means a lot of wastage for us," Munns added.
"It's criminal, to be honest, to be chucking that much food away."
Those "knobbly and misshapen potatoes" however are absolutely fine to eat, she said.
"The only difficulty is peeling them, but just cut the knobbly bit off and peel it separately."
'A challenging period'
Supermarkets including Sainsbury's, Tesco, Morrisons and Waitrose already have dedicated lines for wonky vegetables.
Calum Kelly, Waitrose's produce technical manager, said in demanding weather conditions "we relax size and shape guidelines for key veg to avoid waste and provide more income to our growers and farmers".
"Baking potatoes might be a little smaller than usual this harvest if the drought continues. All these veg still taste great, but like many of us in a heatwave, they might just look a little less than perfect."
Not every gap can be filled this way though. Andrew Opie, the director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium, said supermarkets are also importing more food from abroad as UK supplies run short.
"Retailers face the dilemma of supporting British farmers, but also making sure that we, as customers, have what we expect to buy when we go in the shop," he said.
"It's going to be a challenging period right through into the autumn. We're hearing potentially it could affect things like cherries as well."
British summers are getting hotter and drier as the climate changes and heatwaves like this one are becoming more frequent.
That means a season like this one may become less of a one-off, and more of a preview of what British farming has to deal with regularly.
Many farmers will either have to accept more waste, invest in better irrigation and water storage systems, or find a way to sell more wonky produce to consumers.
Munns, the potato farmer, said more people should try buying imperfect veg if they see it in the supermarket aisle this year.
People should "be a bit less picky" about fresh produce, she said. "We've been too spoilt in the UK … In other less fortunate countries we wouldn't have a choice."

Shirkado Turkish ah ayaa sidoo kale maamula kaabayaal muhiim ah oo Muqdisho ku yaalla, halka labada dowladood ay sanadihii dambe kala saxiixdeen heshiisyo dhinacyada difaaca, badda iyo tamarta ah.
Doorashadan ayaa dhacday iyadoo Soomaaliya ay weli ka jirto khilaaf xooggan oo ku saabsan muddo-xileedka hay’adaha federaalka iyo hannaanka doorashooyinka uu wado Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud.
Puntland, Jubaland iyo qaar ka mid ah mucaaradka siyaasadeed ayaa kasoo horjeeda hannaankaas, iyagoo ku eedeeyey Xasan Sheekh muddo-kororsi sharci-darro ah, halka uu damacsan yahay inuu qabto doorasho aan heshiis lagu ahayn.
Türkiye, oo ka mid ah dowladaha xiriirka ugu dhow la leh Villa Somalia, si cad uma aysan muujin walaac ku saabsan muranka muddo-xileedka hay’adaha dowladda oo dhammaaday, iyadoo Ankara ay sii wadday xiriirkeeda siyaasadeed, dhaqaale iyo amni ee maamulka Xasan Sheekh.
Doorashada loo doortay xilka Guddoomiyaha Golaha Shacabka Soomaaliya, oo muddo-xileedkiisu dhammaaday, ayaa waxaa si buuxda ugu lug lahaa dowladda Türkiye, iyadoo madax sare u soo dirtay Muqdisho muddadii uu socday ololaha kursigan.
Maxamed Cabdulqaadir — oo lagu tilmaamo inuu muddo dheer xiriir dhow la lahaa Ankara — doorashadiisa ayaa markale iftiimisay sida saameynta Türkiye ee Soomaaliya uga soo gudubtay gargaarka, horumarinta iyo tababarka ciidamada, una gaartay xarumaha ugu sarreeya siyaasadda iyo go’aan-qaadashada dowladda.

JOHOR BARU: Reduce outdoor activities and stay hydrated as the prolonged hot and dry spell raises the risk of heat-related illnesses, says state health and environment committee chairman Ling Tian Soon.
He said people should drink more water to prevent dehydration.
Ling also advised the public to choose appropriate clothing during the hot weather, particularly when spending time outdoors.
The Johor Department of Environment (DOE) and local authorities throughout the state would continue monitoring open burning activities amid the hot and dry conditions, he said when contacted.
Ling also spoke about the importance of monitoring the situation to prevent open burning from worsening air quality and to reduce the risk of fires spreading during the dry spell.
Respiratory and internal medicine specialist Dr See Yee Yong said prolonged hot weather could cause a wide range of health problems, from mild dehydration and heat exhaustion to potentially fatal heatstroke.
He said that heat exhaustion and heatstroke would have symptoms such as elevated body temperature, fatigue, profuse sweating, nausea and palpitations.
However, Dr See said heatstroke was much more serious as the body’s cooling system would fail, potentially resulting in confusion or an altered level of consciousness.
“Once someone becomes confused or has a reduced level of consciousness, it should be treated as an emergency and the person should be brought to hospital immediately,” he said.
Dr See said that people generally required about 30ml to 35ml of water per kilogramme of body weight daily, although fluid requirements would increase in hotter weather as the body loses water more rapidly.
“Those who sweat heavily should also replace electrolytes and salts lost through sweating, with isotonic drinks potentially helping to replenish them.”
As for people with existing conditions such as hypertension, heart disease, diabetes and respiratory illnesses, he said they should take additional precautions during the hot weather.
Dr See also advised people with outdoor activities, including construction workers, delivery riders and athletes, to take regular breaks from the heat and get adequate rest.

Kullu: The
monsoon has claimed 163 lives in Himachal Pradesh so far this year, 93 of which were in rain-related road accidents. Other deaths were due to landslides, house cave-ins, rockfalls, flash floods, and snakebites.
Lahaul-Spiti is the worst hit with 14 deaths, followed by Kangra with 12 casualties, Chamba and Shimla with nine each and Kullu with eight deaths. This season, landslides have claimed 14 lives, while 23 people died due to falls.
Around 257 people have also been injured this monsoon.
The cumulative damage between June 30 and Aug 11 has been assessed at Rs 910 crore. Damage to PWD infrastructure alone stood at Rs 686 crore, accounting for 75% of the total loss.
This year’s death toll, grim as it is, is slightly lower than the 180+ deaths during the corresponding period last year. The final monsoon toll in Himachal in 2025 was 448.
Meanwhile, the mountainous state is bracing for more rainfall. An orange alert has been sounded, and rain-triggered landslides and rockfalls have blocked 204 roads.
The Mandi-Kullu and Mandi-Pathankot highways are among the major routes affected, but Kullu and Mandi districts reported the worst impact.
In Anni, two cars were hit by boulders, injuring two persons.
The Mandi-Kullu national highway was blocked near Jhalogi after rocks continued to fall from the hillside. Police stopped traffic as a precaution, stranding vehicles near the Hanogi tunnel, Pandoh Dam and towards Mandi.
Clearance work was also halted due to the continued threat of rockfall. The highway reopened in the afternoon, but traffic remained impacted by rockfalls, leading to its closure again in the evening.
The alternate Bajaura-Kataula-Kamand road that connects Kullu with Mandi also remained blocked on Tuesday. The Mandi-Pathankot highway was also closed near Talghar Urla after a landslide.
All educational institutions in the Kullu subdivision, including schools and colleges, were closed by the administration on Tuesday in view of the heavy rain alert and risk of flash floods.

Temperatures could hit 30 degrees in some parts of the country today.
We're in for another spell of very warm weather, with a status yellow high temperature alert now in place for Tipperary and all of Leinster, lasting until Friday morning.
Met Éireann is warning of heat stress, animal welfare issues, uncomfortable sleeping conditions and water safety concerns as people head to rivers, lakes and beaches.
Cathal Nolan from Ireland's Weather Channel says it could be even warmer than expected. "One or two pockets of Leinster could see temperatures up to 30 degrees, he said.
"It's parts of Leinster that are likely to see the highest temperatures today, for examples areas in and around the greater Dublin area, parts of Kildare, into parts of Carlow, Laois, and Offaly. These areas could see temperatures up close to 30 degrees."
The current hosepipe ban could be extended. Uisce Éireann's head of water operations told RTÉ's Drivetime on Tuesday that some supplies across the country were 'already under pressure' due to the warm weather and that, although parts of the country had seen some levels of rainfall in the last few weeks, "potentially, we could consider extending the water conservation order regionally".
In Britain, prime minister Andy Burnham will chair a meeting of its government’s emergency Cobra committee on Wednesday in response to extreme heat, which has caused widespread wildfires and plunged many parts of the country into drought.
Burnham will meet with ministers, officials and agencies as high temperatures continue across the UK on Wednesday afternoon, with temperatures of 33 degrees forecast and up to 38 degrees on Thursday.
On Tuesday a firefighter union chief warned the country faces a “national emergency” amid ongoing wildfires.
Rare amber “extreme heat” warnings have been issued by the forecaster for London and parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday.
Nearly three quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, after a record dry July and very dry start to August has combined with high temperatures to put pressure on water resources.
